courses.title: Gender Power and Intersectionality
courses.school_name: School of Gender Studies and Gender-Based Violence Prevention
courses.audience: Introductory social work and community-service learners using fictional adult scenarios. This course does not qualify a specialist GBV caseworker, clinician or forensic practitioner; supervised skills assessment and applicable safeguarding procedures remain necessary.
courses.study_guidance: Read each module and use only the supplied fictional adult scenarios. Do not seek real disclosures or submit survivor records for coursework. Write your response before consulting feedback. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise. Supervised skills observation remains a separate requirement.
courses.practice_safety_note: Use only the supplied fictional adult scenario. Do not collect real disclosures or submit survivor records. You may pause or use an alternative fictional exercise. Record your reasoning before checking the learner-guide feedback.
courses.outcome: Analyse a fictional service-access problem through gender, power and intersecting barriers, with an ethical response that avoids blame, forced disclosure and unsupported causal claims.

modules.title: Gender roles power and responsibility
modules.outcome: Distinguish a contextual explanation of unequal access from an excuse for violence or an individual diagnosis.
paragraphs: Gender-related expectations can influence who controls resources, whose decisions carry authority and whose contribution is recognised. Ask how those expectations operate in the particular service or household being discussed rather than assume everyone in a category has the same experience. An ecosocial or demographic description is not a personal diagnosis. The inter-agency standards place survivor-centred support within attention to unequal power and the particular risks faced by women and girls. Non-discriminatory assistance also requires respectful support for anyone experiencing violence, without making access depend on fitting a stereotype about gender, relationships or appearance. [S10, S1]

Power includes more than physical force. A person may face restrictions on money, movement, communication, documents or contact with services. Describe the reported behaviour and its effect on choice or access without requiring a dramatic injury or a complete personal history before offering appropriate support. Responsibility for violence remains with the person using it. Financial hardship, cultural expectations or conflict in a relationship do not justify coercion. The learner's task is to notice an access concern and an appropriate response, not to investigate an allegation, establish criminal liability or direct a survivor's relationship decisions. [S10, S1]

Research can help frame questions but cannot determine what happened to a particular person. The 2026 Nigerian survey analysis uses 2024 data and reports associations among measured contextual factors. Its cross-sectional, self-reported evidence cannot establish which factor caused violence or predict an individual's experience from identity, income or marital status. The paper's outcome wording also leaves uncertainty about the combined time period, so this course does not reproduce a prevalence rate or personal risk score. Ask what the person identifies as a barrier now rather than turn a statistical association into blame or a label. [R23, S1]

In a service review, separate the condition, its possible consequence and the action that the service can authorise. A registration process that requires permission from a partner may restrict a person's independent access. Examine the actual rule, its justification and who can change it, without collecting survivor histories to prove the concern exists. Make disagreement and missing information visible. Provider-perspective research can inform questions about coercion and organisational practice, but it does not prove that a locally revised form will improve recovery. A bounded recommendation should identify a responsible role and the further consultation required. [R22, S10, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: an adult cannot register independently because a service asks for a partner's approval. A learner examines the access rule and decision authority without requesting a violence history, blaming the applicant or claiming that the form alone caused abuse.
modules.activity: Write an access-analysis note with the rule, whose choices it affects, a plausible power concern, missing evidence and an authorised revision route. Include a sentence that keeps responsibility for violence separate from contextual explanation.
modules.feedback: A defensible analysis examines rules and choices without stereotyping people or excusing violence. It distinguishes a service barrier from a legal finding, causal explanation or personal risk classification.

modules.title: Intersecting barriers and meaningful choice
modules.outcome: Analyse interacting access barriers without reducing a person to a list of identities.
paragraphs: Intersectional analysis asks how social positions and systems interact in a particular situation. It is more than adding labels such as age, disability, income, language or location to a form. A person may encounter a combination of inaccessible transport, restricted communication and a service rule that requires repeated visits. The interaction can create a barrier different from any single condition alone. Ask which features actually matter to the decision and whose account is missing. Professional ethics require respect and non-discrimination; no identity category should automatically be treated as evidence of incapacity, consent or a predetermined experience. [S1, S10]

Distinguish a service being listed from a person being able to use it. Cost, opening hours, language, privacy, physical access and the safety of the contact method may affect feasibility. Do not presume that a relative or caregiver is an appropriate interpreter or can give permission for an adult simply because support is needed. Discuss communication preferences and qualified accessible arrangements through the relevant service. The provider-perspective synthesis identifies cultural responsiveness and organisational access as important concerns, but its high-income settings and lack of demonstrated survivor outcomes limit direct transfer to a Nigerian service. [R22, S10]

Informal and formal pathways may both matter, with different possibilities and risks. The Nigerian help-seeking analysis models reported sources of help in 2018 survey data, using a predefined list. Its classes are analytical descriptions, not categories to assign to a current survivor, and the study cannot establish that a family contact is safe or that a listed institution is functioning today. Ask about the person's chosen trusted support and verify the relevant service pathway without automatically involving family, community leaders or police. A preference to delay a referral should not be interpreted as a failure of motivation. [R21, S1]

Make an access map for the fictional task that connects a stated priority, interacting barriers, feasible adjustments, missing information and an accountable role. Use only the information necessary for that task. A useful adjustment might reduce a repeated visit or provide an accessible private contact, but its feasibility must be checked with the service and affected people. Do not infer that one adjustment benefits everyone or that a consultation proves recovery improved. Review who remains excluded and whether the person can still decline or change the proposed next step without losing respectful assistance. [S10, R22, S1]
modules.example: Fictional case: an adult using an inaccessible route also lacks a private phone and cannot attend repeated daytime appointments. A learner examines the interacting barriers, asks about preferred communication and checks an alternative contact arrangement without assuming a caregiver can consent for the adult.
modules.activity: Build a barrier-and-adjustment map for the case. Identify two interacting barriers, one assumption to verify, one access adjustment, an owner and a question that protects meaningful choice.
modules.feedback: The map should connect real features of the fictional situation rather than count identity labels. An accessible arrangement requires verification and individual choice; neither a modelled help-seeking class nor a family relationship establishes safe access.

modules.title: Evidence reflection and accountable access changes
modules.outcome: Prepare an ethical service-access recommendation with explicit evidence and review limits.
paragraphs: Use evidence according to what it can establish. A programme standard describes expected practice, a qualitative synthesis interprets perspectives and a cross-sectional survey examines measured associations. Their strengths differ, and combining them does not turn a proposal into a tested intervention. The Nigerian studies and provider synthesis help learners ask better questions about access and influence; none can determine the experience of everyone using this service. Record the evidence type, relevant context and limitation alongside the recommendation so that a reader can distinguish a useful question from a claim already demonstrated. [S10, R21, R22, R23]

Reflect on the practitioner's own position in the interaction. Control over registration, referrals, funding or information can create pressure even when the worker intends to help. Explain what is optional, what the service can actually provide and which decisions remain with the person. Avoid rewarding disclosure, punishing disagreement or making respectful assistance conditional on accepting a preferred referral. Ethics and survivor-centred programme standards support this approach, while local procedures and lawful limits still need to be understood before a real interaction. An introductory lesson is not permission to invent a reporting rule or promise absolute confidentiality. [S1, S10]

Keep learning and programme feedback separate from a case investigation. Use original fictional scenarios for this course and do not ask classmates or applicants to reveal personal experiences as proof of learning. For an actual organisational review, seek appropriate specialist advice on safe consultation and necessary information rather than collect incident details casually. Aggregate findings can still identify a person in a small group, so consider the context before sharing. Provider perspectives may reveal service problems, but affected people's appropriately gathered views also matter; one professional account should not stand for every survivor's priorities. [R22, S1, S10]

Write a bounded recommendation with the access concern, proposed adjustment, responsible decision-maker, resource dependency, consultation route and review question. State what evidence would show that access changed and what the review cannot establish about violence reduction or recovery. A revised form is an output; more independent use of a suitable service is a different question. Keep unresolved concerns visible and provide an accountable response to feedback. The aim is a feasible ethical improvement that can be reviewed, rather than a universal claim of gender transformation or a certificate of specialist competence based on a short exercise. [S10, S1, R22]
modules.example: Fictional case: a service proposes removing an unnecessary partner-approval field. The learner identifies the approving role and accessible consultation route, then asks whether adults can use the revised process independently. The form change alone is not presented as proof of reduced violence or recovery.
modules.activity: Prepare a recommendation with concern, evidence type and limit, adjustment, approving role, resource condition, feedback route and outcome question. Name one claim the planned review cannot support.
modules.feedback: A useful recommendation makes the decision and its limits visible. It protects choice and privacy, differentiates outputs from outcomes and does not turn short-course completion or an untested adjustment into specialist competence.

modules.title: Gender roles power and responsibility
modules.outcome: Distinguish a contextual explanation of unequal access from an excuse for violence or an individual diagnosis.

teaching_points.text: Gender-related expectations can shape access and authority.
Context does not excuse the person using violence.
Coercion can restrict resources and communication.
Cross-sectional associations do not identify an individual's cause.
Service reviews need proportionate evidence.

modules.title: Intersecting barriers and meaningful choice
modules.outcome: Analyse interacting access barriers without reducing a person to a list of identities.

teaching_points.text: Intersectional analysis examines interaction rather than label counts.
A listed service may remain inaccessible.
A caregiver relationship does not automatically establish adult consent authority.
Modelled help-seeking classes are descriptive.
Delaying a referral can reflect constraints or preferences.

modules.title: Evidence reflection and accountable access changes
modules.outcome: Prepare an ethical service-access recommendation with explicit evidence and review limits.

teaching_points.text: Different evidence types support different claims.
Practitioner control can affect meaningful choice.
Course participation should not require personal survivor disclosure.
Small-group reporting can remain identifying.
A changed form is an output rather than proven recovery.

questions.question: A service requires an adult applicant to obtain a partner's approval. What is a relevant gender-and-power question?

options.text: Whether every applicant has the same household experience.
Whether the rule proves a particular crime occurred.
Whether the rule restricts independent access and who has authority to review it.
Whether a partner's approval is always equivalent to individual choice.

questions.rationale: The analysis concerns the actual rule and its effects on agency.

questions.question: A discussion identifies financial stress around a reported coercive act. What distinction should remain clear?

options.text: Financial stress automatically makes coercion acceptable.
The survivor is responsible for preventing another person's violence.
Context proves that no response is needed.
Stress may be relevant context but does not justify violence or transfer responsibility to the survivor.

questions.rationale: Contextual explanation must not become an excuse or blame.

questions.question: An adult reports that another person controls their documents and service contacts. What is appropriate at this introductory level?

options.text: Recognise the reported access concern and offer a suitable support pathway within role.
Require a visible injury before taking the concern seriously.
Conduct an unsupervised criminal investigation.
Contact the other person to negotiate without permission.

questions.rationale: Support does not require the learner to investigate or confront another person.

questions.question: A survey associates a household characteristic with IPV. What may a learner conclude about an individual with that characteristic?

options.text: Their identity proves that violence occurred.
The association alone cannot establish their experience, cause or personal risk score.
The characteristic excuses harmful behaviour.
The study identifies the correct relationship decision for them.

questions.rationale: Population associations cannot replace a person's account or a suitable assessment.

questions.question: A team wants personal survivor stories to justify reviewing a restrictive form. What is a better first step?

options.text: Ask every applicant to disclose violence publicly.
Assume more sensitive data always improves the decision.
Examine the rule, its access consequences and review authority without soliciting unnecessary disclosures.
Publish a list of applicants who decline to answer.

questions.rationale: A service-rule concern can be examined without collecting unnecessary survivor histories.

questions.question: A person faces inaccessible transport and appointments requiring repeated visits. What should the analysis examine?

options.text: Only how many identity categories appear on a form.
A fixed outcome predicted from one label.
An assumption that the barriers operate independently in every case.
How those conditions combine to affect feasible access.

questions.rationale: Interactions between systems and circumstances can change the practical barrier.

questions.question: A directory names a service but the applicant cannot use its contact format. What remains to assess?

options.text: Whether an appropriate private and accessible contact arrangement is available.
An assumption that listing proves effective access.
Whether the applicant should be blamed for not attending.
A guarantee that every service offers the same adjustments.

questions.rationale: Availability on paper differs from feasible use.

questions.question: An adult needs communication support and a caregiver offers to answer every question. What is appropriate?

options.text: Treat disability as automatic incapacity.
Clarify the adult's preferences and suitable supported communication without assuming substitute authority.
Assume the caregiver's agreement replaces every adult choice.
Exclude the adult from the discussion.

questions.rationale: Support needs and legal authority require distinct consideration.

questions.question: A learner uses a survey's family-help class to decide that every family referral is safe. What is wrong?

options.text: The class guarantees current service capacity.
A survey automatically grants permission to contact family.
The analytical class does not verify an individual's preference or the safety of that pathway.
A model predicts every survivor's next decision.

questions.rationale: A statistical description cannot authorise a specific referral.

questions.question: An adult declines an offered referral today. What should the response preserve?

options.text: A judgement that they are unmotivated.
Withdrawal of all respectful assistance.
An unauthorised referral made secretly.
Respectful support and the opportunity to reconsider, with accurate information and relevant lawful limits explained.

questions.rationale: Choice and circumstances should be explored without coercion.

questions.question: A recommendation cites a standard and a qualitative synthesis. What does that combination alone establish?

options.text: A reasoned basis for questions and practice comparison, with local effects still untested.
Proof of a causal local intervention effect.
The same evidence as a randomised trial.
A universal individual outcome prediction.

questions.rationale: Standards and perspectives do not themselves demonstrate intervention effects.

questions.question: A worker links respectful assistance to accepting the worker's preferred referral. What should be corrected?

options.text: Only the referral form's decorative design.
The coercive condition and the explanation of available choices.
The person's opportunity to disagree.
The need to communicate the service's actual limits.

questions.rationale: A helpful intention does not remove pressure created by conditional assistance.

questions.question: A facilitator asks learners to recount personal violence experiences for marks. What fits this course's design?

options.text: Require disclosure to prove authenticity.
Reward the most detailed private account.
Use the original fictional scenarios and assess reasoning instead.
Publish personal examples in class notes.

questions.rationale: Learning can be assessed without soliciting sensitive personal histories.

questions.question: A feedback summary omits a name but includes a unique role and location. What remains to check?

options.text: A guarantee that removing names ensures anonymity.
Automatic permission to share every detail.
A rule that aggregate labels remove all privacy duties.
Whether contextual details could identify the person before sharing.

questions.rationale: Indirect identifiers can reveal identity in context.

questions.question: A service removes an unnecessary approval field. What outcome question could be reviewed separately?

options.text: Whether intended adults can access the suitable service more independently.
Whether editing a field proves all violence stopped.
Whether the new form certifies clinical recovery.
Whether a completed edit eliminates all need for feedback.

questions.rationale: An access change requires evidence beyond producing the revised form.

courses.cover_title:
